validated_work_order.understanding: Issue #97 carries three non-blocking review findings on PR #94 (for #88), all confined to ReportTableList.test.tsx. ReportTableList.tsx:84 (`key={category.uncategorizedId ?? category.id}`) is correct and stays byte-for-byte unchanged. I reproduced all three on current main by mutating line 84: baseline 4/4 green; `key={category.uncategorizedId}` (fallback deleted) 4/4 green; `key={category.id}` (pre-fix) fails only tests 1 and 2, leaving 3 and 4 green; the filter's `/Encountered two children with the same key/i` is strictly subsumed by `/same key/i`. The prior plan was rejected for asserting that a repaired mixed-sibling test fails under BOTH broken expressions. That objection is correct, and probing further showed it is even weaker than the review stated: React emits the missing-key warning at most ONCE PER TEST FILE, not once per render pass. Verified directly — rendering the same keyless fixture three times in one file yields exactly 1 warning, across both separate render passes inside a single test and across separate tests; reordering so the mixed fixture renders first moves the warning to it (1 then 0); the same fixture in two separate files each gets its own warning (1 and 1). The duplicate-key warning is NOT deduplicated this way (observed 2, 1, 2 across three renders). This makes the single-file design order-dependent: whichever test renders first consumes the warning and every later one passes vacuously — which is why the shipped suite could never guard the deleted-fallback mutant regardless of filter width.
validated_work_order.root_cause: Two independent defects, and fixing the filter alone fixes neither. (1) The console.error filter is pinned to React's duplicate-key phrasing, so a MISSING key — what a deleted `?? category.id` fallback produces for real categories, which have no uncategorizedId — is a different sentence the filter never matches. (2) The missing-key assertion, once added, is inherently order-dependent within a file because React emits that sentence at most once per test file; a second test asserting on it passes vacuously no matter what the key expression does. (3) A fixture whose sibling keys cannot collide under any expression constrains nothing. The fix therefore has to separate the two warning classes into separate files, not merely widen one filter.
validated_work_order.approach: Split the file by warning class rather than widening a single filter, because the two React sentences behave differently: the duplicate-key warning repeats freely, the missing-key warning fires once per test file. (1) Narrow DUPLICATE_KEY_WARNINGS to a single `DUPLICATE_KEY_WARNING = /same key/i` — the second entry was strictly subsumed — and rewrite the comment to record why the loose tail-matching exists and that the exact-sentence pattern was removed precisely because it added nothing. (2) Move the missing-key guard into a NEW file, ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx, matching `/unique .?key.? prop/i`; its comment records the measured once-per-file behaviour, making the deleted-fallback mutant fail reliably rather than only when that test happens to run first. (3) Rename the fixture-reading test and drop its renderRowSpy and uncategorizedId assertions — it read the fixture rather than the component, returning ['other','transfer','off_budget'] for any implementation whatsoever. (4) Repair the mixed-sibling fixture by adding transferRow as a second synthetic sibling plus a matching getByText('Transfers') assertion; the second synthetic row is what collides under `key={category.id}`, since with one synthetic row the fixture cannot fail under any expression. Add a comment above each surviving test naming which half of the expression it guards and which mutant kills it. (5) Fix a latent type bug the edits expose: the fixture helpers spell fields `totalDebits`/`netDebits` but the model declares `totalDebts`/`netDebts`; `tsc-strict` only checks files changed versus main, which is why main is green and the error appears the moment the file is edited.

risks: The change is test-only and touches no production code, so the risk to the app is nil. The risk is in the tests themselves: patterns written too loosely could match an unrelated console.error and fail the suite spuriously, and patterns written too tightly would fail open again — the exact defect this ticket exists to fix. Both patterns are anchored on React's distinctive wording.

Because the filters are now split by file, a missing key elsewhere inside ReportTableList's subtree is only caught by ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx, and only the FIRST such key in that file. A second independent keyless list added later would not be caught by adding a second test to that file — it needs the existing test's fixture widened, or a new file. The comment above the filter records this.

The once-per-file suppression is React-internal and could change across React versions. If a future React emits the missing-key warning per-render again, the split-file design remains correct and merely becomes more conservative than necessary. The reverse (React dropping the warning entirely) would silently void the guard, which is true of any console.error-based approach.

The `totalDebts`/`netDebts` fixture-helper correction changes object literals that previously type-checked only because `tsc-strict` skips unchanged files. The misspelled fields are absent from GroupedEntity/DataEntity, so dropping them can only remove non-existent properties; the helpers still satisfy the types.
No file in forbidden_paths is touched: no .sdlc/memory/**, no docs/spec/**, no .github/**, no .sdlc/**.
No new network host is introduced, so env.api_allowlist in .sdlc/config.yml is unaffected.

validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: Every claim was measured, not inferred. All three review findings reproduced on current main. The prior rejection's central claim was tested directly and found to be both correct and understated (once per file, not once per render pass), and the rejection's own prescribed remedy was tested and shown to be order-dependent — the plan changed because the evidence pointed somewhere better, not to comply with the objection. The proposed design was written and validated against six mutants: three defective ones each fail a distinct, correctly-attributed test, and the two behaviourally-equivalent ones stay green. Order-independence (AC-3) was verified by actually swapping the tests and re-running. tsc-strict, full typecheck, lint, and the wider reports suite (30 files, 499 tests) are all clean. The 8 points held back are for what no local run settles: whether a future React could reword these sentences or change the dedup behaviour, and whether a browser QA pass would surface anything this test-file change does not already cover.
evidence: Baseline on main: `yarn workspace @actual-app/web vitest --run ReportTableList` → Tests 4 passed (4).

Missing-key warning fires ONCE PER TEST FILE, not per render pass. Rendering the same keyless fixture three times in one probe file gave: uuid-only test = 1, uuid+2-synthetic test = 0, two renders inside a single test = 0. So the rejection's stated mechanism ('once per owner/render pass') understates it.
Ordering determines the recipient: a probe whose FIRST test renders the mixed fixture gave 1 warning and whose SECOND identical test gave 0. The warning follows whoever renders first.
Separate files get independent budgets: the identical keyless fixture in two separate probe files each reported exactly 1 warning. This is what makes the split-file design work.

Duplicate-key warnings are NOT deduplicated the same way: three renders under `key={category.id}` reported dup=2, dup=1, dup=2. This asymmetry is why two collision tests can share a file while the missing-key test cannot.

The prior plan's prescribed remedy was built and shown to be order-dependent: swapping the two tests and running `key={category.uncategorizedId}` produced 'Tests 1 failed | 2 passed' only in the original order, while the rejected single-file approach fails 0 of 3 when the mixed test renders first.

Final mutant matrix for this design: baseline 3 passed; `key={category.id}` fails 2 of 3 (both collision tests, named individually); `key={category.uncategorizedId}` fails 1 of 3 ('keys real category rows that have no uncategorizedId'); `key={category.id ?? category.uncategorizedId}` fails 2 of 3; `key={category.name}` and `key={category.uncategorizedId || category.id}` stay green as behaviourally equivalent.

Latent type bug found: fixture helpers spell fields `totalDebits`/`netDebits` but GroupedEntity/DataEntity declare `totalDebts`/`netDebts`. `yarn typecheck` runs `tsc-strict`, which only checks files changed versus main — main typechecks clean, but editing the file surfaces 4 TS2561 errors.
Gates green after the fix: `yarn workspace @actual-app/web tsc-strict` clean, full `yarn typecheck` clean (31s), `yarn lint` clean (2547 files), wider reports suite 30 files / 499 tests passed.
`git diff --stat -- .../ReportTableList.tsx` is empty — the production component is byte-for-byte unchanged from main.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep one file, widen the filter to [/same key/i, /unique .?key.? prop/i], and let the uuid test guard the deleted fallback — the remedy the plan rejection prescribed.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is correct only by accident of ordering. React emits the missing-key warning at most once per test file, verified by rendering one keyless fixture three times in a single file and observing exactly one warning, across two render passes inside one test and across separate tests. Whichever test renders first consumes it, so the guard dies silently if anyone adds a render above it or reorders the file. Measured: with the mixed-sibling test ordered first, the deleted-fallback mutant fails 0 of 3 in that arrangement. Splitting the assertion into its own file is the fix for the mechanism rather than an accommodation of it, and it also removes the temptation to assert the missing-key sentence from two tests in one file, which can never work.

alternatives_considered.approach: Reset React's module-level warning suppression between tests so one file could hold both guards, instead of splitting into two files.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: React exposes no supported way to reset the warning dedup; it would mean reaching into React internals or resetting modules between tests, coupling the suite to an implementation detail of a specific React version that would break the moment that detail changes. A second file costs one duplicated fixture helper pair and depends on nothing but Vitest's default per-file module isolation.

alternatives_considered.approach: Assert on the key expression directly, by capturing the keys React receives instead of watching console.error.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: React keeps keys internal to its reconciler and does not expose them to renderRow, which is exactly why the file reads console.error in the first place. A DevTools fiber walk or a jsx-runtime mock would couple the test to React internals and to the react-compiler transform, both of which change under this repo's setup; a broken transform would then break the guard rather than the code.

alternatives_considered.approach: Delete the mixed-sibling test outright, as the reviewer's first option permits, rather than repairing it.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A repaired fixture is strictly better and I verified it kills `key={category.id}`. Deleting would leave no coverage of a real category and a synthetic row sharing one parent — a list shape the production query layer does produce. The repair costs one added fixture row and one added assertion.

validated_work_order.debate_summary: The brief carried one binding objection against v1: the plan claimed a repaired mixed-sibling test fails under BOTH broken key expressions, and the shipped comment directive named 'which mutant kills it'. I tested the objection rather than accepting it, and it held — then I found it was weaker than stated. React emits the missing-key warning at most once per TEST FILE, not once per render pass (verified: three renders of one keyless fixture in a single file yield exactly one warning, across both render passes inside one test and across separate tests). Duplicate-key warnings are not deduplicated this way. This matters because the rejection's prescribed remedy — keep one file, let the uuid test own the deleted-fallback guard — is itself order-dependent: I built it, swapped the test order, and the guard went silent, letting the deleted-fallback mutant pass 0 of 3. Rather than weaken a claim to match the objection, I changed the design to fix the mechanism: split the file by warning class, so the missing-key guard sits alone in its own file with an uncontested warning budget, which I verified is order-independent. Every acceptance number in this order is a measurement from a run, including the six-mutant matrix.
